 A field guide to wasm-vm

wasm-vm executes a RISC-V computer in Rust and WebAssembly. An unmodified Linux kernel runs above its CPU, memory, interrupt controllers, and virtual devices. Start with the browser demo, then follow the boundary you need to understand.

 Pick a starting point

| You want to… | Start here |
| --- | --- |
| Boot a guest and use its console | [Get started](./docs.html?page=quickstart) |
| Put the machine inside your application | [Embed the machine](./docs.html?page=embedding) |
| Understand CPU, memory, and devices | [Architecture](./docs.html?page=architecture) |
| Keep changes across reloads | [Storage and persistence](./docs.html?page=storage) |
| Connect the guest to a network | [Networking](./docs.html?page=networking) |
| Use the display and input paths | [Desktop and input](./docs.html?page=desktop) |
| Understand admitted guest graphics work | [Graphics boundary](./docs.html?page=graphics) |
| Reproduce a result or contribute a change | [Verification](./docs.html?page=verification) |
| Interpret the published measurements | [Performance](./docs.html?page=performance) |

 Current scope

The public demo loads generated WebAssembly assets and named guest artifacts. The Level 1 report records 395 Sail architectural tests with zero exclusions. Storage, networking, display, JIT, and container work have their own acceptance criteria and evidence; a passing architectural baseline does not make every product surface complete.

 hint style="info" 
The @agent-wasm/ packages belong to a separate host-side project. This repository builds WasmMachine and WasmLinux as relative browser assets. There is no verified @wasm-vm/sdk npm release in this checkout.
 endhint 

 Read beyond the guides

The reference library contains the detailed technical documentation from this repository, including device contracts, renderer boundaries, build runbooks, and dated measurements. Every page exposes its original source and Markdown. Search matches titles, paths, and page content; the Reference section also supports a subject filter.

[Documentation coverage](./docs.html?page=coverage) accounts for every prose file at its pinned migration revision. Current field guides identify newer evidence separately. Task logs, evidence, operating policy, protocols, legal text, and upstream specifications keep their authoritative source intact.

 Product direction

Passkey-encrypted volumes, peer distribution, and the ProofMesh work market are [proposed product work](./docs.html?page=proofmesh). Their specifications are readable here with that scope stated explicitly.

pages.title: Boot your first guest
pages.search:
---
kind: "Field guide"
source: "web/docs-source/guides/quickstart.md"
scope: "Authored explanation; verification belongs to the named evidence"
---

 Boot your first guest

Open the [guest launcher](./index.htmlide) and choose an operating system to run the machine. The demo contains the guest console and display. The [roadmap](./roadmap.html) lives on the main site, and all guides and references are in this documentation library.

 Choose a boot path

 tabs title="Choose the environment" 
 tab title="Public demo" 
The default public manifest supplies the Linux kernel, an initramfs, and a compressed busybox boot snapshot. The loader fetches artifacts and checks their SHA-256 digests. Use the demo's console to inspect the resulting guest.

The full Alpine disk workflow needs its own disk or chunk manifest. A shell in an initramfs is a different environment from an Alpine root filesystem with packages installed.

The checked-in [artifact manifest](./artifacts.json) names exact URLs, sizes, and SHA-256 digests. A compatible compressed boot snapshot can shorten startup; a missing or incompatible snapshot falls back to a cold boot. Read the manifest rather than an old page's copied artifact-size table.
 endtab 
 tab title="Local build" 
Install the Rust target, wasm-pack, and Node/npm prerequisites used by the repository, then build and serve the browser tree:

sh title="Build the browser demo"
make web-build
make web-serve


make web-build builds the generated wasm module, installs pinned browser packages, builds the Docstream reader, and copies the guest ELF fixtures. make web-serve serves web/ on port 8080. In the source layout, / is the machine and /landing.html is the marketing page. The deployable layout moves the machine to /app.html.

For large development images, use bash tools/serve-dev.sh and the relevant image build runbook.
 endtab 
 endtabs 

 What to expect

 stepper 
 step 
Open the demo and choose the required boot mode or image. Artifact sizes and progress come from the manifest and loader.
 endstep 
 step 
Allow the loader to finish fetching and verifying the image. A loaded frame alone is not proof that Linux reached a prompt.
 endstep 
 step 
Use the guest console after it is ready. The selected image determines the available userland and credentials. The Alpine capstone documented in the rootfs guide uses root with an empty password; do not apply that assumption to a different image.
 endstep 
 step 
Choose persistence explicitly for a chunked disk if you want an IndexedDB overlay. Read the storage boundary before treating reload as a save operation.
 endstep 
 endstepper 

 Browser requirements

Serve over HTTP or HTTPS. WebAssembly streaming and ES-module MIME rules do not work reliably through file://. Shared-memory worker/JIT paths require cross-origin isolation; the loader retains a single-threaded path when that boundary is unavailable. Pointer Lock and audio may require a user gesture.

 expandable title="If the guest does not reach a prompt" 
Use the [boot debugging playbook](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-boot-debugging), [desktop bring-up runbook](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-desktop-bringup), and the named artifact manifest. Check the reported error, bytes fetched, digest, and chosen image before changing the guest.
 endexpandable

- [Alpine root filesystem](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-rootfs)
- [Guest kernel](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-kernel)

pages.search:
---
kind: "Field guide"
source: "web/docs-source/guides/architecture.md"
scope: "Authored explanation; verification belongs to the named evidence"
---

 How the machine fits together

The browser runs the emulator. The emulator presents a RISC-V virtual platform. The guest kernel and userland execute above that platform as RISC-V binaries.

 Follow the execution layers

 demo src="architecture/layers" title="Execution layers" description="Select an entry point to see the actual host/guest boundary. This is an architecture explanation." status="Interactive explanation" 

 CPU and memory

The interpreter implements RV64GC plus privileged state and precise traps. Guest virtual memory translates through the emulated MMU; host WebAssembly linear memory holds the guest RAM. The Level 1 report records the architectural compliance boundary for native and WebAssembly builds.

The JIT translates supported blocks. Its ABI, side exits, invalidation, budgets, and floating-point policy are specified separately. A hot-loop diagnostic is not a prediction about a complete Linux workload.

 Virtual platform

The wasm-vm virt platform includes CLINT, PLIC, a 16550-compatible UART, virtio devices, and a goldfish RTC. Device-specific contracts describe what each surface admits and rejects. The device-tree generator and memory map are part of the platform boundary.

The guest retirement clock and browser wall clock serve different purposes. Consult the [timekeeping contract](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-timekeeping) when changing timers, cooperative scheduling, or idle behavior.

 Worker placement

The split-device architecture keeps CPU work and UI/device work behind explicit channels. SharedArrayBuffer paths depend on browser isolation. The worker protocol is an implementation boundary, not an installable public VM SDK.

 hint style="info" 
The 3D homepage model is a cutaway illustration of these layers. Launch the demo for guest execution and use traces or state digests for correctness claims.
 endhint

pages.title: Embed the machine
Storage and persistence
pages.search:
---
kind: "Field guide"
source: "web/docs-source/guides/storage.md"
scope: "Authored explanation; verification belongs to the named evidence"
---

 Storage and persistence

A guest disk is an explicit boot input. The loader supports an initramfs, a whole disk, or a chunked disk. Persistence adds a writable local overlay to a chunked image.

 Select the storage mode

| Mode | Loader behavior | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| initramfs | Pass the manifest initramfs to new WasmLinux | Small public boot path |
| disk | Download the whole rootfs and use WasmLinux.newDisk | A complete local disk image |
| chunked | Fetch a manifest and retrieve disk chunks on demand | Larger image workflows |
| chunked with persist: true | Add an image-namespaced IndexedDB copy-on-write overlay | Local changes across reloads |

The default [artifact manifest](./artifacts.json) supplies the small initramfs boot path. Large Alpine disk and chunked-image workflows require their own development artifacts and local serving setup; the public page does not silently download the full Alpine root filesystem.

 Lazy chunk reads

A missing block read parks the virtio request. The host obtains the required indices through pendingChunks() and services them through fetchPending(). The chunk store verifies bytes before inserting them into its cache.

js title="Use a local chunked image"
const controller = await startLinuxBoot(
  mode: "chunked",
  imageManifestUrl: "./releases/chunked-alpine/manifest.json",
  cacheBudgetMib: 256,
  bootProfileUrl: "./releases/chunked-alpine/boot-profile.json",
  onProgress: (role, loaded, total) => showProgress(role, loaded, total),
);


The boot profile is an ordered first-touch list for read-ahead, not permission to skip chunk verification. controller.fetchStats() exposes the selected chunked path's fetch metrics.

 Immutable base, writable overlay

Base-image chunks are verified against their manifest. The overlay records guest writes as 4 KiB blocks separately in IndexedDB, so the base remains an immutable reference. Flush ordering, recovery, image identity, and cache limits live in the detailed overlay and chunk-format contracts.

js title="Request a persistent chunked guest"
const controller = await startLinuxBoot(
  mode: "chunked",
  persist: true,
  onWriterStatus: ( readOnly ) => 
    console.log(readOnly ? "read-only guest" : "writer guest");
  ,
);


The loader acquires an image-namespaced Web Lock for one writer. A competing tab boots read-only; without the Web Locks API, the persistent path also fails closed to read-only. A durable flush resolves after its IndexedDB transaction completes.

Persistence depends on browser storage availability and policy. A private browsing context, denied storage, quota pressure, or cleared site data changes the retention boundary. Treat an explicit flush and recovery proof as stronger evidence than a page saying it saved.

 Snapshots are a different boundary

A machine snapshot contains CPU, RAM, and device state. A disk overlay contains block writes. Restore must keep those boundaries coherent; a snapshot cannot substitute for a matching image manifest and overlay generation.

The loader checks build identity, image binding, and overlay generation before applying persisted resume state. Missing, incompatible, stale, foreign, or corrupt snapshots produce a typed cold-boot reason rather than silently pairing unrelated state. A snapshot is a boot optimization, not a substitute for artifact integrity.

 Local saved checkpoints

The [demo](./app.html) has a Local saved sessions library. Choose New checkpoint guest to start the pinned, single-hart Alpine software guest with 256 MiB RAM, an instruction-count clock and guest networking disabled. Boot assets are downloaded by the host. This profile keeps recording separate from the ordinary desktop's devices and live connections.

1. Make your guest file changes, then choose Start recording to save the initial point.
2. Choose Checkpoint for another exact restore point. Stop recording saves a final point and ends recording; later changes remain unsaved.
3. Select a session and restore point, then choose Open checkpoint. It restores CPU, RAM, device state, disk changes and pending input together, initially paused. Choose Resume guest to continue. Selecting a preview alone leaves the active guest in place.
4. Rename sessions to distinguish them. A reload or another tab on the same browser origin can reopen the saved points. Opening a point or starting a new checkpoint guest replaces the current guest.

Checkpoints only. The current library restores explicit saved points. Continuous input replay, arbitrary-time seeking, reverse-step and accelerated desktop session history are later Epic 9 boundaries. Recording cannot recover execution from before it started. A session requires its exact compatible runtime, Wasm, kernel and image; an update can leave an older named session visibly incompatible without deleting it.

The demo also has an Execution boundary check. It runs a small guest and compares exact stops, queued-event order and restored counters on the interpreter and JIT. The check reports its result in the page and runs separately from your active guest. It proves the common event-clock mechanism; the saved-session library continues to offer explicit checkpoints.

 Limits, quota and deletion

The library reports saved binary bytes, the browser's approximate origin usage/quota and persistent-storage status. Saved binary data limit counts unique stored chunks once; browser metadata, caches and other site data consume additional space. Restore points per session limits future appends. Lowering either limit preserves existing named history.

Quota or retention failure pauses recording and the guest, preserving the last committed prefix. The status distinguishes unsaved current memory from the saved point. Free space, raise a limit or run Clean up unreachable data, then choose Retry recording to save a new point. Stop recording while quota-paused ends at the committed prefix. Retry refuses history that another tab changed or deleted.

Delete selected session asks for confirmation and removes its restore points. Shared machine chunks and disk data referenced by other sessions are preserved. Cleanup can refuse while another tab holds a writer or restore lease, or when surviving history is incomplete; the status explains the failure and lets you retry. Browser eviction or cleared data appears as incomplete history with Open disabled and Delete available.

Checkpoints are stored locally in IndexedDB on the same browser origin. Names are small display metadata in localStorage. Persistent storage can be requested, but browser denial or later site-data clearing can still remove recordings. Keep an external copy of important guest data; portable session bundle export/import belongs to the later release milestone.

 hint style="info" 
Passkey-encrypted user volumes belong to the proposed ProofMesh product layer. The current IndexedDB overlay is not documented as an encrypted, passkey-owned volume.
 endhint

- [Disk-image pipeline](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-design-image-pipeline)
- [Bounded file transfer](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-design-file-transfer)

pages.search:
---
kind: "Field guide"
source: "web/docs-source/guides/networking.md"
scope: "Authored explanation; verification belongs to the named evidence"
---

 Connect the guest deliberately

The CPU executes locally, while network traffic uses an explicit provider. Downloading boot artifacts and sending guest packets are separate operations; neither is covered by a blanket promise that nothing leaves the tab.

 Guest network path

The virtio-net device feeds the guest network stack. The user-mode slirp implementation supplies the Ethernet/IP boundary, DHCP, and DNS behavior described in its contract. Browser restrictions shape how TCP and UDP reach an external network.

 Provider choices

| Boundary | Documentation |
| --- | --- |
| Slirp user-mode network | [Addressing, DHCP, DNS, and packet handling](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-design-slirp) |
| WebSocket TCP/UDP proxy | [Exact frame protocol](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-design-ws-proxy-protocol) |
| Tailscale worker | [Worker message contract](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-design-tailscale-worker-protocol) |
| Provider deployment | [Identity, endpoints, and teardown](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-deployment-network-providers) |

 Know the trust boundary

A transport provider can observe the traffic carried through it under that protocol's encryption model. Choose endpoints and credentials deliberately. The guest's local execution does not make an external relay local, and an emulator-side packet stack does not remove browser network restrictions.

Use the provider's recorded acceptance criteria to establish supported traffic. A hostname resolving or a link appearing connected is not proof that an application completed an end-to-end exchange.

 Further reading

The [HTTP fast-path evaluation](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-design-http-fast-path-eval) records a dated design investigation. It is not a current claim that every guest syscall or HTTP request bypasses the emulated network stack.

pages.search:
---
kind: "Field guide"
source: "web/docs-source/guides/desktop.md"
scope: "Authored explanation; verification belongs to the named evidence"
---

 Display, input, and audio

The host workbench exposes display and serial surfaces. Guest input passes through explicit keyboard, pointer, clipboard, and audio boundaries. Each boundary has a contract and recorded failure drills.

 Display and guest graphics

Read the display contract before choosing a present path. Desktop bring-up uses named images and a documented boot order. The [current graphics guide](./docs.html?page=graphics) describes Omarchy's qualified GPU warm checkpoint, explicit cold boot, software warm snapshot, and the admitted command, resource, state, shader, and draw boundaries. GPU context-loss recovery has a separate verification task.

 hint style="info" 
The marketing hero is a Three.js architecture illustration rendered directly by the browser. It is independent of guest VirGL support and is not evidence of a guest GPU feature.
 endhint 

 Application image and release scope

The application image contains native RISC-V Chromium 153.0.8010.52, LibreOffice 26.8.0 and Node 26.11.1 / npm 12.2.0 in an 860-package image. These are guest Linux applications, separate from the host browser running the emulator.

The [independent E5.5-T05c verdict](https://github.com/BLamy/wasm-vm/blob/dddae3bc2c15b1332dedcb208f3b7e6c6f852127/evidence/omarchy-applications-desktop/verifier/VERDICT.md) covers actual native Chromium browsing and trusted form input, normal sandboxed SVG decoding, Writer typing/save/close/reopen/edit/resave, Node/npm, and the qualified production compositor and scanout. It retains the original failed attempts and the explicitly authenticated missing-proof continuation; it does not claim that every application rasterizes through the GPU. Its exact source and evidence boundaries remain part of that verdict.

The [application catalogue](https://github.com/BLamy/wasm-vm/blob/dddae3bc2c15b1332dedcb208f3b7e6c6f852127/tools/image/omarchy-apps/catalog.json) accounts for 147 upstream Omarchy 4.0.2 entries: 32 were already present, 97 have native repository packages, five have portable alternatives, and 13 still require source-port work. Chromium and LibreOffice are two explicit additions beyond that list. The 13 unresolved ports are not established incompatibilities, and this is not a claim that all 147 applications are complete.

The [launcher](./index.htmlide) uses matched warm factories for the application image. Accelerated mode restores RAM, disk, GPU resources and the guest clock together. Software mode restores its matching RAM and disk snapshot. Read [guest graphics](./docs.html?page=graphics) for warm, explicit cold and software modes.

Open applications from Omarchy's Apps menu. With keyboard capture enabled, the stock browser shortcut is Super + Shift + B, and Super + Alt + Space opens the Apps menu. Search for LibreOffice Writer, Calc or Impress. The Foot terminal also has node and npm available.

 hint style="info" 
Desktop restoration and application startup are separate measurements. Large guest applications can still take several minutes to start. Chromium's terms dialog and LibreOffice's welcome screens are their genuine first-run interfaces; complete them in the guest when they appear.
 endhint 

 Keyboard capture

The terminal displays whether input is captured for the guest or owned by the browser. Physical KeyboardEvent.code transitions feed the virtio keyboard boundary, while xterm retains its serial text path. Release keys repairs held guest input after focus changes.

Ctrl+Alt+Backquote is reserved for the host view switch. OS- or browser-owned shortcuts can be consumed before the page receives an event; the input contract describes passthrough and recovery behavior.

 Pointer and clipboard

Absolute pointer coordinates use the element's CSS bounds. Relative mode uses Pointer Lock, which may require a gesture or be denied by iframe policy. The fallback returns to absolute mode and releases held buttons.

Clipboard operations are an explicit host permission boundary. Read the clipboard contract before forwarding text or promising synchronization.

 Audio

The browser audio-ring and virtio-snd contracts define the admitted format, control path, and bounded buffering behavior. Browser autoplay policy can require a gesture before audio starts.

pages.title: Guest graphics: the admitted boundary
pages.search:
---
kind: "Field guide"
source: "web/docs-source/guides/graphics.md"
scope: "Authored explanation; verification belongs to the named evidence"
---

 Guest graphics

The accelerated Omarchy path sends the guest's VirGL commands to WebGL2 in the production Linux worker. Mesa chooses OpenGL ES 3.0; Hyprland retries that API after its GLES 3.2 request. Frames reach the visible canvas through retained, fenced scanout and a page presentation receipt.

The command, shader, dimensional depth, transform-feedback and native multisample resolve prerequisites have been independently verified. Recorded production runs cover the real Mesa probe, 1,000 cube frames, Hyprland/Foot scanout and stock desktop typing. Final production deployment and context-loss recovery have separate verification records on the roadmap.

 Launch the desktop

Choose Omarchy in the [launcher](./app), with GPU rendering selected. The worker checks actual WebGL2 limits, texture roles, native renderability and nonzero sampled results before advertising VirGL. An unsupported host produces a visible error; it does not justify positive guest capabilities.

The accelerated image uses a pinned Mesa 26.2.2 build with VirGL and the GLES API exposed through EGL. Its small, recorded source patch makes both border-clamp extension names independently configurable, and rejects desktop OpenGL contexts while retaining GBM's internal buffer-mapping context. It separates multisample renderbuffer support from multisample texture sampling: only qualified two-dimensional color/depth attachment queries can use the measured sample count and format mask. Unsupported border-clamp and sRGB-decode extensions are disabled in both legacy and indexed queries. The software DRI entrypoints are removed.

GPU rendering restores an authenticated Omarchy warm checkpoint on compatible hosts. RAM, the complete disk overlay, the selected guest clock and the original GPU command/DMA journal belong to one pinned artifact. A fresh worker rebuilds actual GPU resources and physically presents the restored display in its new renderer epoch. Readiness also requires new CPU execution; a static desktop can then accept the input that requests another draw. Acceptance checks new guest GPU work after startup. Repeat launches restore an independent copy of the same factory desktop.

The accelerated factory captures a clean session after the original wallpaper and Apps menu have initialized, startup jobs have finished, and disk requests have settled over a measured interval. Preparation opens the stock Apps menu, searches for LibreOffice Writer, closes it and checks the desktop again before freezing RAM, disk and GPU state together.

Use ?guest=omarchy&desktop=1&noSnapshot=1 on the launcher for an explicit GPU cold boot. The Software rendering option retains its paired RAM snapshot and disk delta. BusyBox, Alpine and Alpine + Node keep their fast-boot paths. A corrupt or incompatible GPU checkpoint produces a visible error; it cannot silently become a cold boot or a software session.

 hint style="info" 
An accelerated cold boot starts with instruction-based time. Before its first original keyboard make, including a lock-state repair, it selects host-paced idle. A warm boot preserves the checkpoint's selected mode and exact guest time, then re-anchors its host clock; time spent offline is excluded. Busy execution and JIT timing follow retired instructions, while idle timer jumps are bounded by elapsed host time. Explicit pauses exclude paused time. The software snapshot retains its existing clock policy. The accelerated timing policy is independently verified in E6-T11d72 and E6-T11d73; paired clock restoration is covered by E6-T11d74c.

During instruction-based execution, tickless idle pauses its timer jump while a qualified GPU request awaits the browser, so guest time cannot skip past a pending host fence or presentation receipt. Original keyboard host waits are also guarded. Normal idle advancement resumes when those requests settle.
 endhint 

 What is offloaded

Guest shader translation uses the pinned VirGL TGSI frontend. Admitted commands create retained GPU storage, configure native rendering state and issue actual browser GPU draws. The renderer supports the proven dimensional color/depth views and layer surfaces, uniform buffers, multiple render targets, instancing, stencil operations and original transform-feedback targets.

The production profile has bounded resources and work: 32 MiB per resource or transfer, 128 MiB aggregate GPU storage, one pending queue job, 256 draws and 262,144 index/instance work units per submission. Older isolated proof profiles keep their original limits. Unsupported commands return explicit errors.

Capabilities are typed Rust fields serialized to the pinned 1,408-byte VirGL capset ABI. Reported formats and limits come from host qualification. A feature bit is not inferred from a successful allocation or from the browser's extension string alone.

The page shows completed jobs, draws and transfers for the real guest. The homepage cutaway is a host illustration; it is unrelated to these counters.

 Loss and snapshots

GPU context loss revokes qualification and fails uncertain pending work. Existing CPU display and cursor state remain separate. Restart the accelerated session, or use Restart with software graphics to open the warm desktop.

The accelerated factory checkpoint reconstructs GPU resources from original work; it never serializes native WebGL handles. Its identity includes the runtime, kernel, disk image, host capability profile, complete overlay and component digests. General software snapshot/import APIs still reject accelerated sessions. GPU warm boots currently use an ephemeral disk; persistent software sessions retain their existing snapshot behavior.

 Reproduce the checks

make verify-E6-T11d records the actual VirGL-only Mesa probe, 1,000-frame cube, Hyprland client, original GPU command families and visible scanout. make verify-E6-T11e covers queue lifetimes, deterministic protocol properties and real context loss. Run the named target at its recorded source revision and inspect its evidence digest.

 content-ref url="./docs.html?page=verification" 
How worker evidence and independent verification work
 endcontent-ref 

 content-ref url="./docs.html?page=reference-renderer-virgl-command-readme" 
Original command framing and renderer contracts
 endcontent-ref 

 content-ref url="./docs.html?page=reference-renderer-virgl-shader-readme" 
Shader frontend and admission contracts
 endcontent-ref 

GPU offload does not establish a 300-MIPS or frame-rate claim. CPU throughput and responsiveness require their own browser measurements in the [performance guide](./docs.html?page=performance).

pages.search:
---
kind: "Field guide"
source: "web/docs-source/guides/containers.md"
scope: "Authored explanation; verification belongs to the named evidence"
---

 The container boundary

wasm-vm includes an OCI image pipeline and a guest-side bundle runner. Importing an image, auditing kernel features, and proving a booted container workload are separate acceptance steps.

 Image pipeline

The importer pulls and digest-verifies image content, unpacks a bundle, resolves its entrypoint inside the rootfs, and checks architecture purity. The recorded nine-image matrix covers Alpine, busybox, nginx, httpd, caddy, haproxy, redis, memcached, and postgres.

A matrix PASS means the static bundle checks passed. It does not mean every image booted and served a request inside the emulator. The matrix preserves its survey date and deferred boot leg.

 Guest runner

tools/guest/wvrun.sh consumes a bundle with rootfs/, run.json, and flat config files. The documented runner overlays a read-only lower rootfs with a tmpfs upper, creates namespaces, switches roots, applies the image environment and working directory, and executes the image command.

 hint style="warning" 
The source container audit explicitly separates enabled kernel seccomp configuration from runtime filter installation. Do not present a config flag or static OCI PASS as proof of a complete container isolation profile.
 endhint 

 Check the exact task and evidence

Use the kernel capability matrix and booted acceptance commands to establish what ran. Historical docs can describe a deferred milestone; the current task ledger and evidence determine the status of that exact task. This reader does not turn a historical plan into a newly verified capstone.

 Detailed references

- [Kernel capability audit and runner contract](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-containers)
- [Nine-image static matrix and adversarial self-test](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-container-matrix)
- [Guest rootfs](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-rootfs)

pages.title: Reproduce a claim
pages.search:
---
kind: "Field guide"
source: "web/docs-source/guides/verification.md"
scope: "Authored explanation; verification belongs to the named evidence"
---

 Reproduce a claim

A verification result belongs to a named claim, code revision, command, and evidence digest. The repository separates an implementing worker from a fresh critic so a summary alone cannot close a task.

 Architecture baseline

The [Level 1 report](./docs.html?page=reference-docs-level1-report) records native and WebAssembly RISC-V architectural checks, including 395 Sail tests with zero exclusions. Reproduce its named acceptance with:

sh title="Architecture gate"
make level1-gate


That result establishes the report's architectural boundary. Storage recovery, networking, desktop, JIT workloads, and renderer features require their own acceptance.

 Evidence layers

| Evidence | What it can establish |
| --- | --- |
| Guest instruction trace | The retired instruction sequence and concrete architectural state |
| State digest | A canonical state comparison at a named point |
| Spike / Sail / QEMU differential | Agreement with a named reference under the recorded workload |
| Deterministic native / wasm tests | Asserted behavior exercised by the test input |
| Recorded browser capture | Visible behavior on the built page, with its console and interaction record |

The operating policy's 2026-09-01 update waives host rr traces and retires ssh dev. Proof runs happen on the local machine, with local Docker for Linux-only tooling. Historical runbooks retain their old host commands as records; follow current [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/BLamy/wasm-vm/blob/main/AGENTS.md) for new work.

 Task states

These read-only examples use Docstream's native task markers. Each icon has an accessible state name. They explain the workflow; they are not live task results. The [repository roadmap](./roadmap.html) publishes the actual task ledger.

- [ ] Pending — eligible work has not started.
- [~] In progress — the worker owns the active implementation.
- [?] Implemented / evidence needed — an implementation is submitted, or its proof needs completion. The task file retains the exact implemented or evidence-needed status; this shared icon does not collapse their meaning.
- [b] Blocked — a named dependency prevents acceptance; its repro and blocked_on remain in the task.
- [d] Verification debt — historical landed work is parked outside the active lane, without current exact-head proof. Docstream calls this visual state Parked.
- [!] Refuted — evidence contradicted the claim and semantic rework is required.
- [x] Verified — a separate critic interrogated the evidence and failed to refute the stated boundary.
- [-] Cancelled — the task was explicitly retired or replaced.

The Properties disclosure identifies this guide's authored scope. Reference pages carry their original source revision and SHA-256. Neither a property nor a marked checkbox creates evidence, and this reader cannot edit either. Only the repository's verifier workflow can set verified.

 Local gates

sh title="Local regression gauntlet"
make ci


GitHub Actions is disabled in this repository. Browser bundles build locally; the pre-commit hook maintains deployable web/dist, and Cloudflare Pages hosts the published site. Do not create a GitHub workflow as a substitute for the local proof loop.

 Inspect a result

Read the task's acceptance and the diff before interpreting the evidence.

Predict a concrete state, then check the trace, digest, browser result, or deterministic assertion that could contradict it.
 endstep

Hold changed code against exercised paths. Unexecuted behavior needs evidence; configuration and logging waivers need a reason.

---

 Read the measurements

The homepage publishes two independent Node workload campaigns and a separate native JIT handoff diagnostic. Preserve that separation when comparing a result or proposing an optimization.

 System workloads

web/bench-runtime-workloads.mjs measures file read, file write, stream read, stream copy, server lifecycle, and local HTTP round trips. The recorded policy uses seven measured samples, two warmups, a 1 MiB payload, 64 KiB stream chunks, and eight HTTP requests per sample.

Each measured sample verifies its output digest. File-write timing does not include fsync. A cell carries median, p95, and throughput where bytes were transferred; runtimes can have different storage and network isolation.

[Raw system comparison](./runtime-benchmarks.json) preserves runtime identity, the runner digest, fixtures, policy, individual samples, and unsupported or unmeasured reasons. almostnode's unsupported stream/HTTP cells and WebVM's failed bounded capture remain visible.

 Steady-state compute

web/bench-runtime-compute.mjs keeps one process alive and times deterministic integer, branch, and typed-array loops. Process startup, module loading, and memory reset are outside the timed region. Every warmup and measured sample must match a fixed checksum.

[Raw compute comparison](./runtime-compute-benchmarks.json) retains the publication scope. The main-thread control run is unmeasured because its browser interaction logged a re-entrant WasmMachine error, even though its samples had valid checksums.

 Native JIT diagnostic

The six-op loop tests dispatch-bound behavior; the 64-op loop tests hot-block amortization. Their release-only native MIPS results remain separate from comparable browser measurements. A high hot-loop rate cannot establish a complete guest application rate, file I/O speed, or GUI budget.

 expandable title="Reproduce a small native capture" 
sh title="System workload pre-check"
node web/bench-runtime-workloads.mjs \
  --environment=native-node --samples=7 --warmups=2 \
  --payload-kib=1024 --http-requests=8 \
  --output=/tmp/native-runtime-workloads.json


sh title="Compute pre-check"
node web/bench-runtime-compute.mjs \
  --environment=native-node --samples=7 --warmups=2 \
  --output=/tmp/native-runtime-compute.json


A new native capture is a new result. It does not refresh the older browser campaign by inference.

 Work in the repository

Read the operating manual before taking a task. The queue, roadmap, and verification logs are executable coordination state; documentation style changes must not rewrite their historical claims.

 Choose and prove a task

[AGENTS.md](https://github.com/BLamy/wasm-vm/blob/main/AGENTS.md) defines the worker/critic roles, one-task active lane, dependency gating, risk tiers, evidence requirements, and status transitions. [tasks/QUEUE.md](https://github.com/BLamy/wasm-vm/blob/main/tasks/QUEUE.md) lists eligible work.

Only a fresh verifier can set verified. A worker submits the diff, a concrete claim, and recorded evidence. Run the policy check before regenerating the queue after a task status change.

 Browser changes

Surface browser-reachable capabilities in the demo and roadmap manifest, verify the built page, and retain a screenshot and console result. Build locally. The pre-commit hook assembles web/dist; Cloudflare Pages is the deployment target. GitHub Actions remains disabled.

 Pull requests

The repository uses GitHub-native stacked pull requests through non-interactive gh stack commands. Keep foundational changes below their dependents. A verified task or request to push does not authorize merging; merge only on an explicit current request, following the operating manual.

 Documentation source

The authored field guides live in web/docs-source/guides. npm run check:docs

scope: "Authored explanation; verification belongs to the named evidence"
---

 The proposed ProofMesh layer

ProofMesh is a product proposal above the existing browser machine. Its specifications discuss passkey-owned encrypted volumes, verified peer delivery, and a builder/critic work market. The proposal is not a list of APIs already implemented by wasm-vm.

 Delivery order

1. Freeze schemas, threat models, canonicalization, verifier images, and evidence formats.
2. Prove a local builder/critic loop against a real workload.
3. Add encrypted overlay generations, credential and recovery slots, rotation, and revocation.
4. Add hash-verified delivery from HTTP, cache, and peer sources.
5. Establish diverse critic assignment, attestations, quorum, and challenge windows.
6. Introduce auctions, bounties, accounting, quotas, and abuse controls.
7. Consider process placement across browser nodes only after the storage and evidence boundaries hold.

 Preserve the current boundary

The guest executes locally. The current copy-on-write overlay is not the proposed encrypted volume. The existing provider transport is not proof of a peer distribution network. Recorded acceptance remains the currency for each product surface.

pages.search:
---
kind: "Technical reference"
source: "bench/README.md"
source_revision: "2691b24e6c00478f8d69f81180b6827761de246a"
source_sha256: "54e8124a0bb88c1f92e2cf7988721752d049f872015f4edf6af26f52af36eb55"
scope: "Pinned source; publication does not refresh verification"
---

 In-guest micro-benchmarks: CoreMark + Dhrystone (E4-T03)

 hint style="info" 
Technical reference. Read the stated acceptance boundary and source context before treating a described milestone as current verification.
 endhint 

Automated, reproducible CoreMark and Dhrystone runs inside the guest on the release wasm-vm:
boot → run → parse → emit JSON. This is the micro-benchmark half of the measurement backbone the
capstone's "≥10× CoreMark" threshold stands on, so the workload is pinned (fixed compiler,
flags, iteration counts, committed ELFs) — never apk add-ed at run time, where mirror drift would
silently change what we measure.

 Layout

text title="Layout / 01"
bench/
  toolchain/        pinned Docker cross-toolchain (riscv64-linux GLIBC static gcc)
    Dockerfile        mirrors tools/toolchain/ (digest-pinned Ubuntu + exact apt versions)
    versions.env      the pins (base digest, gcc/glibc versions, build platform)
  guest/
    src/              vendored CoreMark + Dhrystone C sources (+ PROVENANCE.md sha256s)
    coremark.rv64     committed, statically-linked riscv64 ELF (built by build.sh)
    dhrystone.rv64    committed, statically-linked riscv64 ELF
    bench.ext4        committed reproducible ext4 overlay holding both ELFs
    SHA256SUMS        sha256 of the two ELFs (the anti-drift record the harness enforces)
    MANIFEST.txt      image digest, gcc version, flags, SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH
  build.sh            compile the ELFs reproducibly inside the pinned image
  mkimage.sh          pack the ELFs into bench.ext4 (reuses the rootfs mke2fs -d recipe)
tools/bench.py        the harness (boot + console-drive + parse + JSON)


 Running

text title="Running / 02"
python3 tools/bench.py run coremark  --engine native             median-of-3, JSON to stdout
python3 tools/bench.py run dhrystone --engine native --runs 3 --json out.json
python3 tools/bench.py run boot      --engine native --runs 3     macro bench: cold-boot wall clock
make bench-coremark           convenience targets
make bench-dhrystone


The harness builds target/release/wasm-vm if absent (never benchmark the debug build — it is
~100× slower), boots the pinned kernel + Alpine rootfs, attaches bench.ext4 as a second
virtio-blk drive (/dev/vdb), mounts it read-only, runs the ELF bracketed by unique per-run
sentinels, scrapes the score, and powers off. Each cold run takes minutes on the
instruction-stepped interpreter (a full Alpine boot dominates); --runs 3 triples that.

 Run rules & noise expectations

- CoreMark run rules apply: the timed region is ≥ 10 s of guest time (iteration count tuned),
  and the harness rejects any run whose CRC self-check did not print Correct operation validated
  or whose seedcrc is not the standard performance-run 0xe9f5.
- Dhrystone score is DMIPS = dhrystones/sec ÷ 1757 (VAX-11/780 reference). The harness
  validates the benchmark's own end-of-run integrity values (Int_Glob==5, …) before trusting it.
- Spread: the harness reports median-of-N plus (max−min)/median and sets noise_warning
  when that exceeds 5 . In practice the spread is tiny (see the honest-time note below): the score
  is derived from guest-elapsed, which is a deterministic function of retired instructions, so it
  barely moves run-to-run.

 Honest emulator-time framing (why the timing check is a ratio, not 1:1)

The guest CLINT mtime advances from the retired-instruction count (clock_div=10, 10 MHz
timebase), not from host wall-clock. So the guest's clock_gettime/time() — and therefore
CoreMark's "Total time" and Dhrystone's elapsed — are a deterministic function of instructions
executed, decoupled from how fast the host actually ran them. This is by design (it is what makes
native and wasm agree instruction-for-instruction).

Consequently:

- The score (iterations/sec, DMIPS) is essentially host-speed-independent and highly
  reproducible — good for detecting a real ≥10  codegen/interpreter change.
- A naive "guest-elapsed vs host-wall must match within 5 " check would false-positive constantly.
  Instead the harness records guest_elapsed_s, host_elapsed_s, and their ratio, and flags
  deviation from a per-benchmark baseline ratio (BASELINE_RATIO in tools/bench.py).

Tamper case (adversarial 2). Suppose someone patches the guest (or the emulator's
clock_div) so mtime advances twice as fast — the guest then reports half the elapsed time and
the score doubles. Guest-elapsed halves while host wall-clock is unchanged, so the host/guest ratio
doubles and trips RATIO_TOLERANCE_PCT → timing_check.flagged=true. A silent 2× clock lie
cannot pass. Symmetrically, a throttled host (adversarial 3) raises host-wall-clock, moving the
ratio the other way — the harness reports the change rather than caching a stale number.

To set the baseline: run once on an idle reference machine, read timing_check.ratio, and put it in
BASELINE_RATIO. It is an anti-cheat signal only — it never alters the reported score.

 Reproducible builds (AC4)

text title="Reproducible builds (AC4) / 03"
bench/build.sh               build the ELFs (builds the pinned image if absent)
bench/build.sh --no-cache    from-scratch image rebuild, then compare SHA256SUMS


Byte-identical rebuilds come from: the digest-pinned Ubuntu base + exact apt gcc/glibc versions +
fixed build platform (amd64, regardless of host arch), plus SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH,
-ffile-prefix-map (no build-path leaks), -g0, and strip. The committed ELFs + SHA256SUMS
are the durable artifact; the image is how you reproduce them. mkimage.sh packs them into
bench.ext4 with the reproducible mke2fs -d recipe (fixed UUID + hash seed, E2FSPROGS_FAKE_TIME,
^metadata_csum, normalized mtimes) borrowed from tools/rootfs-inner.sh.

The harness enforces the pins at run time: it refuses to run unless each ELF's sha256 matches
SHA256SUMS and bench.ext4 exists (adversarial 4 — a deleted/tampered overlay fails loudly
instead of silently benchmarking a different binary from the base rootfs).

 Boot macro benchmark (E4-T04)

run boot wall-clocks a cold boot with byte-pattern-defined endpoints (not eyeballed):

- t0 = the genuine first UART byte written by the guest. This VM's SBI prints no OpenSBI
  banner (SBI impl ID 0x574d = "WM"), so the first console output is the kernel's earlycon
  line — captured by Console.wait_first_byte, the engine-identical start endpoint.
- t1 = the getty login: regex on the serial console. boot_wall_s = t1 − t0.

It boots with no second drive and --profile-boot, which halts the VM at the login marker (no
shell interaction / kill needed) and prints a PROFILE_JSON … line on stderr. Its total_retired
is recorded as boot_retired_instrs — the retired-instruction count at getty-login (median of
the runs). It is a near-deterministic, host-noise-free anchor: honestly it is not bit-exact —
it jitters ~0.2 because the profiler stamps the retired count in the console-feed quantum where
login: is first seen, a boundary not instruction-aligned to the exact login byte (the boot
execution itself is instruction-count deterministic by design). The harness asserts the anchor is
stable within 1 across runs; more movement would signal real nondeterminism. boot_wall_s is
the only host-noisy metric →
median-of-3 with the same spread / noise_warning reporting as the micro-benches. Schema fields:
unit:"seconds", higher_is_better:false, plus boot_retired_instrs.

 Ledger — append-only, hash-chained baseline history (E4-T04)

bench/ledger.json accumulates every recorded baseline/measurement. It is append-only and
tamper-evident via a per-entry prev_sha256 hash chain.

text title="Ledger — append-only, hash-chained baseline history (E4-T04) / 04"
python3 tools/bench.py run boot --engine native --ledger --baseline level3-interpreter
python3 tools/bench.py record out.json --baseline level3-interpreter    append an existing result
python3 tools/bench.py report                                           per-bench history + speedup
python3 tools/bench.py report --bench boot                              one bench
python3 tools/bench.py report --verify                                  walk chain; nonzero on break


Schema. "schema_version": 1, "entries": [ … ], written back with
json.dumps(ledger, indent=2, sort_keys=True). Each entry:

text title="Ledger — append-only, hash-chained baseline history (E4-T04) / 05"
 bench, engine, score, unit, higher_is_better, spread,
  commit,             emulator git HEAD at measurement time
  vm_build,           "release"
  baseline,           e.g. "level3-interpreter" (null for ad-hoc runs)
  config,             the run's config block (flags, iterations, kernel/rootfs, …)
  date,               ISO-8601 UTC
  prev_sha256        sha256 of the PREVIOUS entry's canonical JSON (json.dumps(entry, sort_keys=True))


The first entry's prev_sha256 is a fixed genesis constant (64 zeros). record/run --ledger
never reorder or rewrite existing entries — they only append. report --verify recomputes the
chain and validates the required keys, exiting nonzero on any break: mutating one historical entry
breaks the next entry's prev_sha256 link and is detected (adversarial 4).

 Performance-regression gate (E4-T27)

tools/bench_ci.py turns the ledger into a merge-blocking invariant: a regression fails
the build. Noise is fought with four layered mitigations (all standard practice):

1. Interleaved A/B (bench_ci.py run): rebuild + run the baseline commit and the candidate
   commit alternately in one job, compare ratios not absolutes — a throttled host scales
   both arms equally, so the verdict is invariant (unit-tested test_ab_host_variance_immune).
2. Robust statistics: median-of-5 with MAD outlier rejection (robust_center) — a single
   hiccup run cannot move the verdict.
3. Two-tier response: soft WARN at > 3 , hard FAIL at > 7 , plus absolute
   latency budgets (JIT pause p100 < 5 ms, MMIO/echo/keystroke budgets) whose breach is an
   unconditional hard fail.
4. Rolling-best baseline moved ONLY by explicit tools/bench.py bless (no silent
   ratchet-down); the trend page surfaces cumulative sub-threshold drift.

Thresholds live in bench/thresholds.toml (every bench + latency metric, soft/hard bands,
gate = gating|advisory — native gates, browser is advisory until the pinned-Chromium runner
lands). The statistics + threshold-eval core is pure and unit-tested (no benchmark run):

text title="Performance-regression gate (E4-T27) / 06"
python3 tools/bench_ci.py selftest                        16 unit tests (or python3 tools/bench_ci_test.py)
python3 tools/bench_ci.py evaluate --candidate s.json     the CI gate: exit 1 on hard fail
python3 tools/bench_ci.py run --baseline-commit <ref> …   live interleaved A/B (needs the runner)
python3 tools/bench_ci.py trend --out bench/trend.html    static dashboard from the ledger
python3 tools/bench.py bless coremark --score S --rationale "why"    promote a new baseline


evaluate samples JSON: "metrics": "<metric>": "candidate": [..], "baseline": [..] —
omit baseline to take it from the ledger's latest entry for that bench. Runner setup
(frequency pinning, warmup, browser-version capture) is in bench/RUNNER.md; the drop-in CI
job is .github/workflows/perf-regression.yml (the unit job always runs; the live perf
job needs the dedicated perf-runner). bless records an auditable bless block
(rationale, blessed_by, supersedes_score) and appends through the same hash chain, so
report --verify stays green and any historical tamper is still detected.

 Browser engine — reaping-deferred

--engine browser is intentionally not run here. The Alpine browser boot OS-reaps on the
development mac (see the E3 memory note "Browser Alpine boot reaped on mac"), so the browser path is

 Perf-regression runner setup (E4-T27)

 hint style="info" 
Technical reference. Read the stated acceptance boundary and source context before treating a described milestone as current verification.
 endhint 

The performance gate (tools/bench_ci.py) turns benchmarks into a merge-blocking invariant.
Its trustworthiness depends on a low-noise, pinned runner. This is the operational recipe;
provisioning the box is CI-admin / dev debt (see the ticket's Verification debt).

 Why a dedicated runner

Shared GitHub-hosted runners are co-tenanted and thermally variable — exactly the conditions
that produce false perf failures. The gate mitigates noise in software (interleaved A/B ratios,
median-of-5 + MAD outlier rejection, two-tier bands), but the last mile — demonstrating 10
consecutive no-op runs with zero false fails (AC2) and <1 spurious hard-fail across 25 runs
in a day (adversarial 2) — can only be shown on the actual runner class. Do not claim those
ACs green on a shared mac; this repo's mac also OS-reaps multi-minute boots (see the E3 memory).

 Runner class

- Label the runner [self-hosted, perf-runner] (matches .github/workflows/perf-regression.yml).
- Dedicated physical box or a pinned isolated VM — not shared with other CI.
- Pin CPU frequency governor to performance; disable turbo/boost for repeatability
  (cpupower frequency-set -g performance; echo 1 > /sys/devices/system/cpu/intel_pstate/no_turbo).
- Pin the process to isolated cores (taskset/cset shield); no other tenants on those cores.
- Capture provenance every run: uname -a, rustc --version, and the browser version.

 Warmup

- One untimed warmup boot before the measured series (drops cold-cache first-run outliers).
- The A/B runner already interleaves baseline/candidate so slow thermal drift hits both arms
  equally; still, let the box idle to a steady thermal state before the job.

 Browser benches (pinned headless Chromium)

- Browser metrics (mmio_, echo_latency_, keystroke_) are advisory in
  bench/thresholds.toml until this is stood up — they warn, never fail the build.
- Pin the exact Chromium build (e.g. via @sitespeed.io/browsertime or a vendored revision),
  record chromium --version into the run artifact, and only then flip their gate to
  gating in thresholds.toml.

 Local / offline invocation

text title="Local / offline invocation / 01"
 gate logic (no benchmark run — pure math, always available):
python3 tools/bench_ci.py selftest

 evaluate recorded/synthetic samples against thresholds (CI gate contract, exit 1 = hard fail):
python3 tools/bench_ci.py evaluate --candidate samples.json

 live interleaved A/B (needs the runner + built release wasm-vm):
python3 tools/bench_ci.py run --baseline-commit <ref> --metrics coremark,dhrystone,boot --pairs 5

 promote a new rolling-best baseline (requires a rationale; no silent ratchet-down):
python3 tools/bench.py bless coremark --score <s> --rationale "<why>"

 trend dashboard from the ledger (one command):
python3 tools/bench_ci.py trend --out bench/trend.html

 E4-T19 — cross-browser WebAssembly module-cost matrix

 hint style="info" 
Technical reference. Read the stated acceptance boundary and source context before treating a described milestone as current verification.
 endhint 

Measures the per-WebAssembly.Module / per-Instance fixed costs the JIT's batching strategy is
designed around (docs/jit-architecture.md §7): compile latency vs module size (1..256 functions),
instantiate latency, memory per module, and the live-instance cliff (1k / 5k / 10k). These are the
numbers that justify the batching K and the E4-T20 budgets.

 Run (one command)

text title="Run (one command) / 01"
./run.sh


Installs the Playwright browsers, serves this directory, and runs the matrix on Chromium,
Firefox, and WebKit (the Safari substitute — no macOS CI runner). Output lands in
results/<engine>.json.

 What it measures

- genModule(n, bodyOps) (gen-module.mjs) emits a valid WASM module of n exported functions
  sharing one memory — the SHAPE of a JIT batch module — so byte size scales with function count.
- harness.html runs, per engine: median WebAssembly.compile and WebAssembly.instantiate over a
  size sweep, a 31-sample fresh-instance first-execution probe against the 5 ms E4-T06 pause target,
  then instantiates up to 10k live instances of a 64-func module to find the cliff (records
  failedAt, wall time, and performance.memory.usedJSHeapSize where available — Chromium only;
  null elsewhere, documented per row). A bounded follow-up may override the targets and
  output directory without changing the canonical run:

  
  E4_T19_CLIFF_TARGETS=10000,25000 \
    E4_T19_RESULTS_DIR=results/cliff-2026-09-02-corrected-25k \
    npx playwright test --project=chromium --project=firefox --project=webkit
  

  E4_T19_CLIFF_TARGETS accepts positive integer counts; every target is released before the next
  one, so the probe measures a held live set rather than accumulating prior tiers. The extended
  result directory is intentionally separate from the clean-checkout results/.json matrix.
- cost-matrix.spec.mjs drives the page in each browser and writes the JSON.

 Optional cross-version screen

The committed three-engine command uses pinned Playwright browser revisions. For a second Chrome
installation, set E4_T19_CHROME_EXECUTABLE and run the added chromium-system project:

text title="Optional cross-version screen / 02"
E4_T19_CHROME_EXECUTABLE='/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome' \\
  npx playwright test --project=chromium-system


This writes results/chromium-system.json; it is supplemental robustness evidence, not part of the
clean-checkout three-engine matrix.

 Status (verification debt)

The committed rows were re-captured after fixing the harness to retain actual WebAssembly.Instance
objects. The canonical run reaches the requested 10,000 target in WebKit, while Chromium fails after
122 live instances and Firefox after 999 with an out-of-memory error. The corrected 25,000-target follow-up reaches
25,000 in WebKit and reproduces the Chromium/Firefox limits; the supplemental Chrome 152 screen
fails at 124. Production BrowserExecutor now caps live batches at 24, which is more than 4x below
the conservative 122-instance Chromium result. The true WebKit cliff beyond 25,000 and
independent-machine K robustness remain verification debt; the first-execution probe is recorded
and stays below the 5 ms E4-T06 target on every tested engine/version.

 Supplemental Linux screen

For a separate browser/OS environment on the same host, the corrected matrix can be run in the
arm64 Linux Playwright image used by the committed supplemental rows:

text title="Supplemental Linux screen / 03"
repo_dir="$PWD"
docker run --rm --init --ipc=host \
  -v "$repo_dir/bench/module-costs:/src:ro" \
  -v "$repo_dir/bench/module-costs/results/cliff-2026-09-02-linux:/out" \
  -w /work \
  mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.62.1-noble \
  bash -lc 'set -e
    mkdir -p /work
    cp /src/harness.html /src/gen-module.mjs /src/cost-matrix.spec.mjs /src/playwright.config.mjs /src/package.json /src/package-lock.json /work/
    npm ci --no-audit --no-fund
    E4_T19_RESULTS_DIR=/out npx playwright test --config playwright.config.mjs --project=chromium --project=firefox
  '


The output directory is intentionally separate from the canonical clean-checkout matrix. Docker
reports the image as arm64 Linux; this is supplemental same-host evidence, not an independent
physical-machine result.

 hint style="info" 
Historical record. Numbers and verdicts belong to the original run and its stated revision, host, and workload; publication here does not refresh that verification.
 endhint 

Tests whose DUT-vs-reference signature comparison is permitted to differ, each with a
spec-cited justification. Target: EMPTY by the Level-1 capstone (E1-T24) — now MET.

 Status: EMPTY — the full arch-test suite passes (395 / 0) against the Sail reference

Every entry that lived here existed for ONE reason: the Spike fallback reference
(spike-1.1.1-dev) could not be configured to our exact declared ISA. Spike hardcodes
misaligned trapping, and its ISA/extension set could not be pared to Bare/Sv39/Sv48 + 16-entry
PMP, so signatures diverged on tests our machine handles correctly for the ISA it declares.

E1-T26 switched the reference to the canonical RISC-V Sail model (sail_riscv_sim, a
config-honoring golden model), with compliance/sail/sail_config_override.json pinning Sail to
our declared ISA (rv64gc + S/U + Sv39/Sv48/Sv57; misaligned scalar supported;
Svnapot/Svpbmt/Svrsw60t59b disabled). Against that reference the entire suite passes with 0
failures, so there is nothing to exclude:

- Misaligned load/store (8 privilege/misalign-) — our machine supports hardware
  misaligned access (hw_data_misaligned_support: True); Sail honors the declaration and
  agrees. (Spike could not — it always traps misaligned.)
- Sv57 (formerly 38 vm_sv57 / vm_pmp/sv57) — the DUT now implements Sv57 (5-level
  page walk, satp MODE=10; E1-T28), so Sail is left with Sv57 enabled (its default): the
  vm_sv57 / vm_pmp/sv57 tests genuinely run the 5-level walk against BOTH and their signatures
  match. No longer excluded. (Was previously excluded when the DUT capped at Sv48.)
- 64-region PMP (4 pmpm_all_entries_check) — our machine declares 16 PMP entries; the
  64-region case is gated off by the DUT platform and Sail matches.

The Spike fallback remains available (RISCOF_REF=spike bash tools/run_riscof.sh) and still
reports its documented 43 divergences — a reference-capability gap, not a DUT bug, which is
exactly what moving to the canonical reference resolves.

 hint style="info" 
Technical reference. Read the stated acceptance boundary and source context before treating a described milestone as current verification.
 endhint 

Minimized repros distilled from divergences the lockstep comparator + fuzzer found. Each entry is
the exact prior architectural state + RAM + block that made the JIT (wasmtime master) disagree with
the shadow interpreter (Hart::exec_oracle).

 Layout
- .repro.txt — human-readable divergence reports (seed, minimized block, prior register/RAM
  state, and the block's disassembled wasm bytes). Everything needed to reproduce OFFLINE (AC5).
- The replayable cases live as Rust literals in
  crates/jit-runtime/tests/lockstep_fuzz/corpus.rs and are replayed by the corpus_replays_clean
  regression test on every run. With the CORRECT translator they must lockstep-CLEAN; they are the
  exact operand shapes that DIVERGE the instant the corresponding bug is reintroduced.

 Provenance
The current corpus is seeded from the mutation-adequacy sweep (the deliberate, never-shipped
translator bugs behind the mutation-testing cargo feature). sraw-wrong-shift-mask.repro.txt is a
verbatim capture of the AC2 killer-gate run: the fuzzer caught a mis-translated SRAW (64-bit
arithmetic shift instead of the W form) at program 11 / block 3 and auto-minimized it to a single
instruction. Reproduce the whole sweep with:

text title="Provenance / 01"
cargo test -p wasm-vm-jit-runtime --features mutation-testing --test lockstep_fuzz -- --nocapture


 Adding a new repro
When the fuzzer finds a NEW divergence (injected or, more valuably, real):
1. Save its report() text here as <slug>.repro.txt.
2. Add its minimized block + prior state to tests/lockstep_fuzz/corpus.rs::cases() so
   corpus_replays_clean guards it forever.

 wasm-vm-wasm-emit (E4-T07)

 hint style="info" 
Technical reference. Read the stated acceptance boundary and source context before treating a described milestone as current verification.
 endhint 

Hand-rolled WebAssembly module emitter — the byte-level backend the JIT (E4-T09…T20) calls at
runtime to turn a translated guest basic block into a real .wasm binary and instantiate it via
WebAssembly.compile (one module per ~64-block batch, per docs/jit-architecture.md §7).

It is not a RISC-V → WASM lowering (that is the JIT's job). It is the generic, correct, fast
builder underneath: LEB128, section framing, and a typed opcode API.

 Why hand-rolled

wasm-encoder+friends would work, but this code runs inside a wasm module in the browser, is on
the JIT hot path, and is small enough to own — exactly as v86 owns src/rust/wasmgen. So:

- no_std + alloc, zero runtime dependencies (cargo tree -p wasm-vm-wasm-emit -e normal shows
  only this crate). Builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown and native.
- wasmparser + wasmtime are dev-dependencies only — they validate and execute the output in
  tests; they never enter the shipped wasm build.

 API shape

rust title="API shape / 01"
use wasm_emit::;

let mut m = ModuleBuilder::new();
let t = m.add_type(FuncType::new(&[ValType::I64, ValType::I64], &[ValType::I64]));
let f = m.add_function(t);
m.export("add", ExportKind::Func, f);

let mut b = FuncBuilder::new(&[ValType::I64, ValType::I64]);
b.local_get(0);
b.local_get(1);
b.i64_add();
m.add_code(b.finish());

let bytes: Vec<u8> = m.finish(); // a valid wasm binary


- leb128 — write_u32/u64/i32/i64, minimal-length by construction.
- types — ValType, RefType, BlockType, Limits (incl. shared-memory flag 0x03),
  Mutability, MemType, TableType, GlobalType.
- module::ModuleBuilder — type/import/function/table/memory/global/export/element/code/start
  sections in canonical order with size prefixes measured from the finished bytes.
- func::FuncBuilder — one method per opcode (full i32/i64 ALU/compare/shift, all load/store widths
  with memarg, local./global., call/call_indirect, structured control with blocktypes,
  br/br_if/br_table, select, memory.size/grow, and the threads-proposal atomic subset).
  Local indices and control-flow balance are checked at build time.

 Safety / hard-to-misuse

- Out-of-range local.get/set/tee panics at emit time.
- Unbalanced end (extra or missing) panics — an unbalanced body can never reach a module.
- Section length prefixes are written after the content exists, so a nested change can never
  invalidate a pre-computed prefix (the classic size-fixup bug).

 Benchmark

tests/speed.rs emits a 200-function × 1000-instruction module and asserts < 10 ms native.

Measured on this machine (Apple Silicon, unoptimized debug test build):

text title="Benchmark / 02"
emit 200 fns / 400000 instrs -> 601445 bytes in 3.84 ms  (156.7 MB/s, 104.2M instr/s)


That is ~52k function-emits/sec even unoptimized (release is materially faster); the assertion bound
is 10 ms. See the test's eprintln! for the live number.

 Validation

cargo test -p wasm-vm-wasm-emit runs:

- tests/leb128.rs — golden edge bytes (0, 127, 128, ±64, i32::MIN, u64::MAX, i64::MIN/MAX),
  20k-case round-trip + minimality property tests, and a per-shift boundary sweep.
- tests/validate.rs — the four required module shapes (add; funcref table + call_indirect;
  loads/stores + locals + control flow; 64 functions), an executable wasmtime smoke test, the
  adversarial cases (≥32-deep nesting, 1000-target br_table, 60k locals, body-length LEB boundary),
  API-misuse panics, and a 10 000-module randomized-straight-line property test — all validated
  by wasmparser::Validator with the threads feature on.
- tests/speed.rs — the emit-speed sanity bound.

 Release assurance boundary

 hint style="info" 
Operating policy. The complete authoritative source is retained at its stated revision. Publication does not change task status, release assurance, or the verification rules.
 endhint 

wasm-vm does not wait for all roadmap tasks before it can ship. “Fully tested and secure” is not
a terminal state; releases make a bounded claim against a named threat model and keep regression
walls running afterward.

 v0.1 — persistent networked Alpine

The first supported release boundary is the verified Epic 3 capstone (E3-T28), not completion of
Epics 4–7. It includes the verified Level 1 architecture, Level 2 boot/platform boundary, and the
Epic 3 persistence/network/browser path needed to boot and use Alpine. Acceleration, GUI, SMP,
sharing, and box64 remain experimental future features and do not block v0.1.

A v0.1 release candidate requires:

- E1-T24, E2-T26, E3-T19, E3-T26, E3-T27, and E3-T28 verified at their exact submitted heads;
- no active refuted, implemented, or evidence-needed release-boundary task;
- the full native/WASM architecture regression wall green in CI;
- fresh-profile browser boot with zero application console errors;
- persistence recovery, explicit network-provider identity, HTTPS egress, secret audit, and
  deployment teardown evidence;
- a dependency/license/CVE scan recorded for the release commit;
- documented known limitations and an incident/reporting contact.

verification-debt outside this boundary does not block v0.1. Debt within the boundary must be
verified, removed from the supported claim, or explicitly listed as a release blocker.

 After release

High-risk changes continue to use the full adversarial charter. Medium- and low-risk changes use
the tiered policy in AGENTS.md; broad workspace, compliance, stress, and cross-target suites run
in CI/nightly. A release claim is revoked when a standing regression wall or supported-boundary
security proof becomes red.

 ADR 0002 — SBI firmware: built-in Rust SBI, OpenSBI kept as an M-mode testcase

 hint style="info" 
Technical reference. Read the stated acceptance boundary and source context before treating a described milestone as current verification.
 endhint 

Status: accepted (E2-T03) · Date: 2026-07-05
Deciders: wasm-vm Epic 2 · Spec target: RISC-V SBI v2.0

 Question

Who is the M-mode firmware under a Linux kernel?

- (a) Built-in SBI — the emulator is the firmware (TinyEMU/JSLinux style). ecall
  from S-mode is answered in Rust; no guest M-mode code on the boot path; the kernel is
  entered directly in S-mode.
- (b) OpenSBI as guest payload — run an unmodified OpenSBI fw_dynamic/fw_jump
  in M-mode on the emulated hart, exactly as hardware would.

 Evaluation — both options were prototyped and RUN (not argued)

 Prototype (b): real OpenSBI v1.3 on our machine

tools/adr0002_opensbi_probe.sh extracts the QEMU-distribution
opensbi-riscv64-generic-fw_dynamic.elf (v1.3) and boots it on our emulator
(crates/core/tests/boot_contract.rs::opensbi_fw_dynamic_boots): loaded at
0x8000_0000, a0=hartid 0, a1= our own E2-T02 DTB, a2=fw_dynamic_info
magic "OSBI", version 2, next_addr 0x8020_0000, next_mode S, CLINT + PLIC attached,
16550 stub on UART0.

Run 1 transcript (verbatim, first bytes of console output):

text title="Prototype (b): real OpenSBI v1.3 on our machine / 01"
OpenSBI v1.3
   ____                    _____ ____ _____
  / __ \                  / ____|  _ \_   _|
 | |  | |_ __   ___ _ __ | (___ | |_) || |
 | |  | | '_ \ / _ \ '_ \ \___ \|  _ < | |
 | |__| | |_) |  __/ | | |____) | |_) || |_
  \____/| .__/ \___|_| |_|_____/|___ /_____|
        | |
        |_|

sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap handler failed (error -2)
sbi_trap_error: hart0: mcause=0x0000000000000007 mtval=0x0000000088000015
sbi_trap_error: hart0: mepc=0x0000000080002ab0 mstatus=0x8000000a00007800
[... full register dump printed by OpenSBI's own trap handler ...]


What this proves empirically:

- The banner printed. Real OpenSBI ran thousands of M-mode instructions on our hart —
  CSR setup, trap installation, it parsed our E2-T02 DTB to find serial@10000000
  (ns16550a) and drove our UART stub through polled LSR/THR. This is the strongest
  independent consumer test our M-mode + DTB have had.
- The trap was OUR bug, precisely diagnosed by OpenSBI itself: mcause=7 (store
  access fault) at mtval=0x8800_0015 — 21 bytes past the end of 128 MiB DRAM. Our
  dtb_placement put the DTB flush against top-of-RAM; OpenSBI's reserved-memory fixup
  grows the DTB in place. Fixed in E2-T03: fdt::DTB_SLACK (16 KiB headroom above the
  blob). Run 2 (after the fix) is recorded below.
- Notably, the probe got further than the pessimistic case in the task text ("requires
  PMP and medeleg/mideleg semantics to be flawless" — they were: 64-entry PMP, counters,
  and delegation CSRs all held up under real firmware).

Run 2 (after the DTB-slack fix): OpenSBI boots COMPLETELY and hands off to S-mode.
Key lines of the 2197-byte transcript (re-runnable: bash tools/adr0002_opensbi_probe.sh):

text title="Prototype (b): real OpenSBI v1.3 on our machine / 02"
Platform Name             : riscv-virtio,qemu          ← read from OUR DTB
Platform Timer Device     : aclint-mtimer @ 10000000Hz ← our TIMEBASE_FREQ_HZ
Platform Console Device   : uart8250
Platform Reboot Device    : sifive_test                ← our test@100000 node
Runtime SBI Version       : 1.0
Domain0 Region00..03      : [PMP domains programmed]
Domain0 Next Address      : 0x0000000080200000
Domain0 Next Mode         : S-mode
Boot HART Base ISA        : rv64imafdc
Boot HART PMP Count       : 64                          ← our E1-T27 PMP, detected
Boot HART MIDELEG         : 0x0000000000000222
Boot HART MEDELEG         : 0x000000000000b109
=== outcome: MaxInstrs, final pc 0x80200000 ===          ← parked in our stub kernel


OpenSBI's own hart init lands on exactly the mideleg 0x222 / medeleg 0xB1FF this
ADR's boot contract specifies — independent confirmation of the delegation table below.

 Prototype (a): built-in SBI first call

boot_contract.rs::builtin_sbi_first_call_and_reset_state: the machine enters a
hand-assembled S-mode payload per the boot contract below; the payload issues the kernel's
canonical first SBI call (Base probe, a7=0x10); the built-in dispatcher answers
SBI_ERR_NOT_SUPPORTED (-2) (skeleton semantics — Base lands in E2-T04) in a0, 0 in
a1, and execution resumes at the next instruction in S-mode (proved by a sentinel
li ra, 42 after the ecall and RunOutcome::MaxInstrs in the parking loop, no M-mode
excursion, no trap escape).

 Decision

(a) Built-in SBI, implemented in Rust in the emulator (SBI v2.0). The kernel is entered
directly in S-mode; ecall-from-S is dispatched by crates/core/src/sbi.rs.

AND: OpenSBI stays as a standing M-mode compliance testcase — the probe above is kept
runnable (tools/adr0002_opensbi_probe.sh, ignored test in boot_contract.rs), so we keep
the M-mode coverage option (b) would have given us without paying its costs on the boot
path. This satisfies the "fallback plan" requirement: option (b) is not rejected as
infeasible — it demonstrably boots to its banner — it is simply not the default path.

 Why

- Debuggability. Every SBI call is a Rust breakpoint away; no bisecting through a
  200 KB opaque binary during Epic 2 bring-up (the probe's own trap illustrates the
  difference: OpenSBI's register dump is nice, but the fix was in our Rust either way).
- Hot path. No M-mode guest instructions between the kernel and its timer/console —
  matters in the browser, where every retired instruction is interpreter work.
- The queue already builds it. E2-T04 (Base + DBCN + legacy console), E2-T05 (TIME),
  E2-T06 (IPI/RFENCE/HSM) implement the extensions; this ADR fixes their dispatch shape.
- We keep the authenticity check anyway via the standing OpenSBI probe.

 Costs / consequences

- We own SBI v2.0 spec compliance (probe semantics, error codes, HSM state machine) —
  E2-T04..T06 acceptance criteria carry that.
- M-mode sees less real-world traffic in the default path — mitigated by the standing
  OpenSBI probe and the RISCOF privilege suites (395/0 vs Sail).
- The mcounteren/medeleg reset contract is ours to state (below) rather than
  inherited from OpenSBI's hart init.

 The boot contract (E2-T15 implements against exactly this)

Set by Machine::boot_supervisor(hartid, dtb_addr) (crates/core/src/lib.rs), asserted
instruction-zero by builtin_sbi_first_call_and_reset_state:

| State | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| privilege | S-mode | no M-mode guest code on this path |
| pc | KERNEL_BASE = 0x8020_0000 | platform::virt::KERNEL_BASE, DRAM+2 MiB (fw_jump convention) |
| a0 | hartid (0) | standard Linux/SBI handoff |
| a1 | DTB physical address | from fdt::dtb_placement (top of DRAM − blob − 16 KiB slack, 8-byte aligned) |
| mideleg | 0x222 | SSI/STI/SEI delegated to S |
| medeleg | 0xB1FF | causes 0..=8 (incl. illegal-instr + load/store access faults) + I/L/S page faults → S (OpenSBI's full set; wide by necessity — no guest M-mode, so mtvec stays 0) |
| satp | 0 (Bare) | kernel builds its own tables |
| sstatus.SIE | 0 | interrupts masked until the kernel opts in |
| PMP | entry 0 = R/W/X NAPOT over all memory | S-mode needs an explicit grant |
| M-mode CSRs | unreachable from the guest | S-mode kernel cannot access M CSRs (arch-enforced); the emulator host owns them |

SBI calls: a7=EID, a6=FID, args a0..a5; return a0=error / a1=value; unknown or
unimplemented EID → SBI_ERR_NOT_SUPPORTED (-2), never a trap (asserted by
sbi::tests::unknown_eid_is_not_supported and the prototype).

 Extensions Epic 2 implements (SBI v2.0)

| Extension | EID | Task |
|---|---|---|
| Base | 0x10 | E2-T04 |
| Debug Console (DBCN) | 0x4442434E | E2-T04 |
| legacy console putchar / getchar | 0x01 / 0x02 | E2-T04 |
| TIME | 0x54494D45 | E2-T05 |
| IPI (sPI) | 0x735049 | E2-T06 |
| RFENCE (RFNC) | 0x52464E43 | E2-T06 |
| HSM | 0x48534D | E2-T06 |
| SRST (system reset; Linux 6.6 probes at init — critic finding) | 0x53525354 | E2-T06 |

 Revisit conditions

- A kernel or userland stack that requires vendor SBI extensions we don't want to own.
- Epic 6 SMP: if per-hart HSM in Rust proves harder than delegating to OpenSBI, re-run the
  probe (it should by then reach next_addr cleanly) and reconsider (b) behind a flag.
- Any divergence between our SBI behavior and OpenSBI's observed behavior in the standing
  probe is a bug in ours until shown otherwise.
